title: Storage accounts: choose, protect, replicate, and move data
summary: Design a school document archive by choosing storage services and account settings, separating redundancy from recovery, configuring selective object replication, and planning encrypted, authorized transfers.
priorityReason: The AZ-104 study guide effective April 17, 2026 explicitly includes configuring storage accounts, redundancy, object replication, encryption, Storage Explorer, and AzCopy. These are practical administration decisions, not a prediction of exam question frequency. First-party sources were checked on September 20, 2026.
officialObjectives: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy.

lessons.title: Choose a service and account before uploading anything
lessons.summary: Translate familiar documents, shared folders, messages, and records into Azure services, then make account choices that do not quietly remove a required feature.
objectives: Match a storage service to the way an application reads and writes data.
Distinguish account kind, performance, redundancy, and blob access tier.
Apply account naming and endpoint rules without treating an address as permission.
Choose a flat or hierarchical namespace and plan account creation with explicit constraints.

sections.title: A storage account is not a folder on a remote PC

blocks.text: Imagine the school office has PDFs of old newsletters, a shared folder of current forms, and a website that processes document uploads. Moving all of these to the cloud does not mean choosing one enormous remote disk. Azure Storage offers services with different ways to store and retrieve information. A storage account is the Azure resource that groups supported services under a name and configuration. It is not a Microsoft Entra user account, and creating it does not create a Windows computer that you must patch.

A subscription supplies the billing and administration context. A resource group collects related Azure resources for management. Within that group, the storage account has its own region, performance configuration, redundancy setting, networking rules, and encryption configuration. A blob container is a grouping inside the account's Blob service. A PDF stored inside that container is a blob. Keep the hierarchy straight: subscription, resource group, storage account, container, blob. A container here is not a containerized application.

Account boundaries matter because important settings are shared. You cannot give one container LRS and another container GZRS inside the same account. Those are redundancy choices, explained in the next lesson. Separate accounts can also separate test material from confidential records, different regions, or incompatible features. However, creating an account per document would add unnecessary administration. Choose boundaries around real differences in ownership, security, resilience, or workload, and then organize related objects with containers and names.

sections.title: Choose the interface the application actually needs

blocks.caption: A service is chosen by the operation, not by the file extension alone
rows: Applications upload, download, and address objects through web APIs. A blob has content and associated properties and metadata.
Keep scanned newsletters and PDF documents in a private document container.
A managed file share offers file-system access through supported SMB or NFS protocols. Protocol and account support must be checked.
An office program expecting a shared drive uses an SMB file share rather than being rewritten to call a blob API.
An application places messages in a queue; another process retrieves messages and performs work later.
After an upload, queue a request to generate a document preview. Store the document itself in Blob Storage.
Store structured, nonrelational entities identified by partition and row keys. This is not a relational database with ordinary SQL joins.
An application can record simple document-processing status keyed by school year and document identifier.
Blob Storage gains a hierarchical namespace and file-system operations useful to analytics engines.
A later analytics project processes directories of school statistics. This is a namespace decision, not a new performance tier.

blocks.text: SMB means Server Message Block, a common Windows file-sharing protocol. NFS means Network File System, widely used with Linux. An API, or application programming interface, is the set of operations software calls to work with a service. The school website can use Blob Storage without mounting a drive. Conversely, an old office application that insists on file paths may fit Azure Files better. Similar-looking filenames do not make those access methods interchangeable.

Blob types also describe behavior. Block blobs suit documents and other ordinary objects. Append blobs suit append-oriented writes, such as adding log entries. Page blobs support random updates to ranges of data and are associated with disk-oriented workloads. Do not infer that every feature supports every blob type: object replication, later in this module, supports block blobs, not append or page blobs. Azure managed disks are separately managed resources; choosing premium page blob storage is not the usual instruction for creating a managed VM disk.

sections.title: Separate account kind, performance, and access tier

blocks.text: For a new mixed-purpose storage account, standard general-purpose v2 is the usual starting point. Its account kind is StorageV2. It supports Blob, Files, Queues, and Tables, with capabilities subject to the selected service and configuration. Premium accounts are specialized, SSD-backed options for workloads needing low latency or high transaction performance. Premium does not mean every standard feature plus faster hardware. It can mean fewer services, fewer redundancy choices, and no standard blob access tiers.

blocks.caption: Interpret kind and performance together
rows: Broad service support and standard block-blob tiering. Suitable for the school's ordinary document archive.
Specialized for block and append blobs. Not an Azure Files account and not a way to obtain GRS.
File shares only. Use the documented supported SMB or NFS configuration, not blob operations.
Page blobs only. StorageV2 by itself therefore does not prove standard performance or broad service support.

blocks.text: SKU means stock keeping unit, the product configuration Azure records. A value such as Standard_ZRS combines standard performance with zone-redundant storage. It is not the same as the kind StorageV2. The hot, cool, cold, and archive blob access tiers instead describe storage and retrieval cost tradeoffs for eligible data. Hot is not a synonym for Premium, and Archive is not an account kind. Archive data is offline and must be rehydrated before ordinary reads; the word archive in our school project name does not require using the Archive tier.

Do not plan an arbitrary in-place switch from a standard account into a premium block blob or premium file account. Such a change normally means creating an appropriate account and migrating data. Documented upgrades from legacy general-purpose v1 or legacy BlobStorage accounts to general-purpose v2 are a separate case. New designs should use current supported account types rather than copying an old tutorial's classic deployment model. A portal preference for a storage workload guides the creation experience; it does not by itself disable other services supported by the chosen account type.

sections.title: A valid name becomes part of a service address

blocks.text: Storage account names contain between 3 and 24 characters, using only lowercase letters and digits, and must be unique across Azure. A hyphen that is acceptable in many resource group names is not acceptable here. The fictional candidate schoolarchive26 has 15 characters: school has 6, archive has 7, and 26 contributes 2, so 6 + 7 + 2 = 15. That satisfies the character and length rules, but only Azure's availability check can confirm that the name is unused. Never assume an example account belongs to you.

With standard public-cloud endpoints, the Blob service address follows https://ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net and the Files service follows https://ACCOUNT.file.core.windows.net. Replace ACCOUNT with an actual authorized account name. A blob address adds a container and object name after the Blob endpoint. The Data Lake endpoint uses dfs rather than blob. Use endpoint values reported by the actual account when working in other Azure clouds or with special endpoint configurations; do not hard-code an IP address that DNS currently returns.

An endpoint is where a request is sent, not a permission slip. A URL containing a school's account name does not grant anonymous access. Network rules must allow the connection and the service must authorize the requested data operation. Signing into the school website is another application-level event; it does not automatically grant the browser direct access to Azure Storage. These distinctions prevent a common mistake: making a private archive public just because a correctly formed URL returned an access error.

blocks.title: Use standard endpoints for this design
blocks.text: The account overview currently labels Azure DNS zone endpoints as preview and says they enter retirement in March 2027. This module uses standard endpoints, not that preview. This endpoint feature is unrelated to choosing a public or private DNS zone for the school's own domain.

sections.title: Folder-shaped names are not always real directories

blocks.text: In a flat namespace, a blob named newsletters/2026/september.pdf has slashes in its name. Tools can display those prefixes like folders, but the namespace does not provide the same real directory object as an ordinary file system. Moving an apparent directory can require processing the blobs whose names begin with that prefix. For a simple website that stores object names in a database and downloads individual PDFs, this is often entirely adequate.

A hierarchical namespace, abbreviated HNS, adds real directories and directory operations to Blob Storage through Data Lake Storage capabilities. Renaming a directory can update its directory entry rather than renaming every object separately. Directory-level access control lists, or ACLs, can express permissions along a file-system hierarchy. That helps analytics systems that write into directories and rename them as jobs finish. It does not turn the account into Azure Files, and it does not mean a familiar folder display alone justifies enabling HNS.

This decision has compatibility consequences. Once HNS is enabled, you cannot revert the account to a flat namespace. Eligible existing accounts have a documented upgrade process, but that is not a casual reversible checkbox. The current feature matrix marks blob versioning, change feed, and object replication as unsupported with HNS enabled. Enabling NFS or SFTP also changes the supported feature set. The standard account can still have supported redundancy and encryption options, but those do not restore a feature that the namespace removes.

blocks.prompt: The school wants automatic block-blob object replication next term. Someone proposes enabling HNS now because Storage Explorer shows folder icons. Is that a harmless presentation change?
blocks.answer: No. Keep a flat namespace for this replication design, or separate the analytics workload into another suitable account.
blocks.explanation: HNS changes namespace behavior and feature compatibility, not merely icons. Current object replication requires versioning and source change feed, and the feature matrix does not support those features on HNS-enabled accounts. Folder-like blob prefixes already provide the basic organization the archive needs.

sections.title: Worked example: turn requirements into creation settings

blocks.title: Plan the newsletter archive without deploying it
blocks.scenario: The school website stores private PDF newsletters as block blobs. It needs ordinary online reads, tolerance of a zone outage, future selective object replication, and no analytics directory operations. Assume the chosen region supports Standard_ZRS. This is a paper configuration exercise, not an instruction to provision Azure resources.

steps.action: Record the intended subscription, resource group, region, owner, and synthetic-data-only test scope before opening the creation form.
steps.why: These decisions establish billing ownership, administrative boundaries, regional availability, and what data may be used. A resource group's location does not substitute for choosing the storage account's region.

steps.action: Choose standard general-purpose v2, kind StorageV2, with the Standard_ZRS configuration.
steps.why: Standard block blobs fit ordinary PDFs. ZRS meets the stated zonal resilience requirement in the assumed supported region. Premium would need an actual latency or transaction justification, not the label 'important documents'.

steps.action: Validate an available lowercase alphanumeric account name, select standard endpoints, and leave HNS, NFS, and SFTP disabled for this workload.
steps.why: The name must be valid and unused. The flat namespace preserves the feature path needed for later versioning, change feed, and object replication.

steps.action: Plan private containers, require secure HTTPS transfer, and specify a permitted network path and Microsoft Entra data authorization for the website's identity.
steps.why: Container privacy, transport protection, network reachability, and identity permissions solve separate problems. Do not rely on one to supply the others.

steps.action: Keep Microsoft-managed encryption unless a documented key-control requirement calls for customer-managed keys, and choose recovery settings deliberately.
steps.why: Data is already encrypted at rest. Key ownership is not deletion recovery, and redundancy is not a substitute for versioning, soft delete, or a tested backup design.

steps.action: Review the proposed configuration and cost assumptions, then stop before Create. Record how a later authorized administrator would verify the deployed properties.
steps.why: A paper exercise can fully explain the choices without spending money. In a real deployment, checking the actual kind, SKU, namespace, security settings, and data operations is stronger evidence than merely seeing 'deployment succeeded'.

blocks.result: The plan meets the stated online, zonal, and future replication requirements. It deliberately does not promise regional disaster recovery, Archive-tier compatibility, automatic object replication, or access for every signed-in user.

sections.title: Verify configuration separately from useful data access

blocks.text: After a real authorized deployment, inspect the account Overview and configuration pages to confirm the region, account kind, performance, redundancy, and namespace. Inspect Networking and Encryption separately. Then use a harmless test object through the intended client path. A successful account creation is a management-plane result. A successful upload and download demonstrates data-plane access for that identity and path. A failure in the second test does not necessarily mean the account was created incorrectly.

Estimate cost from stored capacity, transactions, tier-specific retrieval, redundancy, regional transfer, and enabled extras. A small current dataset can accumulate a large version history if frequently overwritten. Object replication also stores another copy and performs operations at both ends. Premium and standard billing differ, so compare the real workload rather than an account name. Budgets and alerts notify people; they do not normally stop every charge automatically. Retention and narrow cleanup should be designed before any optional exercise.

blocks.title: Read the requirement before selecting the familiar option
blocks.text: A shared-drive requirement points toward Azure Files; document objects accessed by web APIs point toward Blob Storage. StorageV2 is a kind, Standard_ZRS is a configuration, and Hot is an access tier. A directory analytics requirement may justify HNS, but an object replication requirement currently rules HNS out. Resolve conflicting requirements rather than selecting all features.

checkpoints.prompt: An existing office program must continue using an SMB shared drive. It is not being rewritten to call object APIs. Which service matches that interface?

choices.text: Azure Files with a supported SMB configuration.
choices.explanation: Correct. Azure Files supplies the file-share interface the unchanged application requires.

choices.text: A blob container, because both services can store PDFs.
choices.explanation: A PDF extension does not determine the access protocol. A blob container is not automatically an SMB share.

choices.text: Queue Storage, with each document treated as a processing message.
choices.explanation: A queue coordinates work through messages. It does not provide the application's shared-drive interface.

checkpoints.explanation: Choose a service from the required operations and protocol, not just from the kind of content.

checkpoints.prompt: A new account must support ordinary block blobs, queues, and tables. Which proposed configuration fits those services?

choices.text: Standard general-purpose v2 with a supported redundancy configuration.
choices.explanation: Correct. Standard StorageV2 supplies the requested service mix.

choices.text: Premium FileStorage because Premium contains every standard service.
choices.explanation: FileStorage is specialized for file shares. Premium is not a universal superset.

choices.text: StorageV2 with Premium performance, without checking its supported services.
choices.explanation: That identifies the premium page blob account configuration, not the broad standard service mix. Kind and performance must be interpreted together.

checkpoints.explanation: Standard general-purpose v2 is the suitable mixed-service account; specialized premium accounts solve different problems.

checkpoints.prompt: Which statement correctly evaluates the fictional candidate schoolarchive26?

choices.text: Its 15 lowercase-letter-and-digit characters meet the syntax rules, but availability still needs checking.
choices.explanation: Correct. The count is 6 + 7 + 2 = 15, within 3 to 24. Global uniqueness is a separate condition.

choices.text: It is usable if no other account in this resource group has the name.
choices.explanation: Uniqueness is across Azure, not merely inside the resource group.

choices.text: It must become school-archive26 because account names require separators.
choices.explanation: Storage account names allow only lowercase letters and digits. Hyphens are not allowed.

checkpoints.explanation: Naming validation checks both syntax and Azure-wide availability. A teaching example is not a reserved name.

checkpoints.prompt: The school must use native object replication for its block blobs. It only needs folder-like organization, not analytics directory operations. Which namespace decision fits current support?

choices.text: Keep a flat namespace and organize blob names with prefixes.
choices.explanation: Correct. Prefixes provide the needed organization without enabling a namespace that currently excludes object replication.

choices.text: Enable HNS and switch it off whenever replication runs.
choices.explanation: HNS cannot be reverted to flat, and native object replication is not supported on HNS-enabled accounts.

choices.text: Enable HNS on a premium block blob account to bypass the restriction.
choices.explanation: The HNS restriction also applies to premium block blob accounts. Paying for premium does not remove it.

checkpoints.explanation: A compatible set of features matters more than enabling the greatest number of options.

takeaways: Choose Blob, Files, Queue, or Table from the workload's interface and behavior.
Read account kind, performance, redundancy, and access tier as separate settings.
A valid globally available account name and a correct endpoint do not grant data access.
HNS supplies real directory semantics but is irreversible and currently excludes object replication.
Verify management configuration, data access, recovery needs, and cost assumptions independently.

lessons.title: Know which copies exist, when they are current, and who can use them
lessons.summary: Select account redundancy for failure scenarios, reason about asynchronous regional recovery, and configure a separate rule-based relationship for eligible block blobs.
objectives: Compare LRS, ZRS, GRS, GZRS, and their read-access variants.
Explain recovery point exposure and the limitations of planned and unplanned failover.
Configure object replication prerequisites, policies, rules, and selection scope.
Distinguish replicated availability from deletion recovery and verify network and feature compatibility.

sections.title: Copies protect against particular failures, not every mistake

blocks.text: Redundancy means Azure maintains multiple copies so a hardware or location failure need not destroy the only copy. Durability concerns retaining data; availability concerns whether requests can succeed now. They are related but different. Data might survive in a secondary region while the application still cannot write to it. Likewise, multiple healthy copies of an accidentally overwritten document faithfully preserve the wrong current content. Redundancy is not a history of every good state.

A region is an Azure geographic deployment area. An availability zone is an independently powered, cooled, and networked location within a supporting region. Locally redundant storage, LRS, maintains local copies within a datacenter in the primary region. Zone-redundant storage, ZRS, synchronously distributes copies across availability zones in the primary region. Synchronous means a successful write waits for the required replication. Applications still need retry handling for temporary network changes during a zone failure; resilience does not mean every individual request can never fail.

Geo-replication adds an asynchronous copy into the account's paired secondary region. Asynchronous means a primary write can succeed before that update reaches the secondary. The primary region determines the paired secondary; GRS is not a menu for choosing any destination region. Each account's redundancy setting applies to its exposed storage services, subject to those services' support. If two workloads need genuinely different redundancy configurations, plan separate accounts rather than trying to set redundancy on individual blobs.

sections.title: Build the names from three independent questions

blocks.caption: Normal operation before failover, for supported standard account services
rows: Asynchronous transfer, then local redundancy there.
Not normally readable or writable by the application.
Same asynchronous regional pattern as GRS.
Read access to a potentially older state; not writes.
Asynchronous transfer, then local redundancy there.
Not normally readable or writable by the application.
Same asynchronous regional pattern as GZRS.
Read access to a potentially older state; not writes.

blocks.text: Read the table by asking: how are copies arranged locally, is there a second region, and can clients read that second region before failover? RA changes the last answer, not the synchronous-versus-asynchronous behavior. GZRS does not make the secondary zone-redundant: its secondary uses local redundancy. A secondary Blob endpoint has -secondary after the account name. The application must deliberately use it or have an appropriate retry strategy. An RA setting alone does not rewrite the school's application or make the secondary writable.

blocks.title: One RA-GZRS account, with a delayed regional copy
blocks.description: The primary service writes synchronously across its availability zones. The regional transfer is asynchronous. The secondary group is locally redundant and can serve authorized reads with RA enabled, but cannot accept application writes before promotion through a supported failover.

nodes.label: School application
nodes.detail: Normally reads and writes the primary

sections.title: Qualify the service, account type, region, and tier

blocks.text: Do not treat the six options as available on every account. Standard general-purpose v2 supports the broad redundancy family, but ZRS and GZRS availability depends on region. Premium block blob and premium file accounts use supported LRS or ZRS configurations, not the geo-redundant family. Azure Files does not expose an RA secondary for direct reads even when the containing standard account uses a read-access configuration for other services. Standard file shares and premium file shares also differ in their supported redundancy.

For standard block blobs, the Archive access tier supports LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS, not ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS. Therefore, 'must stay online through a zone failure' and 'must use Archive in this same account' conflict. Keep the active online archive on ZRS or a suitable geo-zone configuration, and put separately designed offline archival data in another compatible account if necessary. Premium block blob accounts do not provide the standard hot, cool, cold, and archive tiering model.

blocks.title: Do not turn a broad table into an unsupported deployment promise
blocks.text: At the review date, the account overview mentions ZRS for premium page blobs, while the account-creation and redundancy type tables list premium page blob creation with LRS. This module does not promise premium page blob ZRS availability. Verify the current specific account creation support in the target region. Our worked configurations use standard general-purpose v2 and explicitly assume their named redundancy option is supported.

blocks.title: Configure regional read resilience in a new account plan
blocks.scenario: The school now requires primary-zone resilience and an independently readable regional copy of online block blobs. Assume the target region supports RA-GZRS, the account is standard general-purpose v2, and no Archive-tier or object replication requirement applies.

steps.action: In the paper account-creation plan, select Standard performance and a supporting primary region.
steps.why: A premium account or unsupported region would remove the needed geo-zone configuration before any read-access choice could help.

steps.action: Select geo-zone-redundant storage and enable the option that makes read access available in the secondary.
steps.why: GZRS supplies primary-zone plus regional protection. Enabling secondary reads makes the resulting configuration RA-GZRS rather than plain GZRS.

steps.action: Review the resulting configuration as Standard_RAGZRS and record the paired secondary region and reported secondary Blob endpoint.
steps.why: Checking the resulting setting catches a missed read-access option. The secondary region is determined by the primary, not freely selected in this account's redundancy setting.

steps.action: Plan an authorized secondary read test after initial replication, without initiating failover or writing to that endpoint.
steps.why: A successful secondary read proves the application's chosen read path works. It neither proves zero lag nor supplies a writable disaster-recovery endpoint.

blocks.result: The new-account plan explicitly configures the required redundancy rather than relying on a default. Changing an existing account is a separate conversion task: check its supported conversion path, feature restrictions, and completion state instead of assuming every redundancy pair is an immediate reversible switch.

sections.title: Worked example: calculate the uncertain recovery window

blocks.title: A regional outage during newsletter uploads
blocks.scenario: A standard RA-GZRS account supports the chosen region. It has no object replication policy or other failover-blocking feature. At 10:12 UTC the primary becomes unavailable. Last Sync Time is 10:05 UTC. Uploads finished at 10:03, 10:07, and 10:11. These times are hypothetical observations, not an Azure replication guarantee.

steps.action: Classify the failed location as the whole primary region, not just one zone.
steps.why: Zonal copies help with a zone outage. A regional outage requires the separately replicated secondary and an application recovery plan.

steps.action: Compare each completed upload with Last Sync Time.
steps.why: The 10:03 write is before 10:05 and is covered by that synchronization boundary. The 10:07 and 10:11 writes are later and may not have reached the secondary. Last Sync Time does not prove every later write is missing.

steps.action: Calculate 10:12 minus 10:05 as seven minutes of potentially unsynchronized writes.
steps.why: This measures the observed exposure window. It is not seven minutes of guaranteed lost data, and it says nothing about how long restoring application service will take.

steps.action: Let an appropriately designed read-only view use the secondary endpoint while administrators assess recovery.
steps.why: RA-GZRS permits authorized secondary reads. The view must tolerate older or absent recent documents and must not advertise a successful new upload to that read-only destination.

steps.action: Evaluate an unplanned account failover only after checking eligibility, business approval, and potential data loss.
steps.why: Failover redirects service endpoints and promotes the secondary; it is not a per-document restore. Unsynchronized primary data can be lost, and the new primary becomes LRS after customer-managed unplanned failover.

blocks.result: The school can distinguish confirmed replicated history from uncertain recent writes. It has a read-access option, not a zero-loss or instant write-recovery guarantee. Restoring geo-redundancy and checking replication again are separate follow-up tasks after unplanned failover.

blocks.prompt: Before failover, a teacher changes the upload destination from the failed primary endpoint to the RA-GZRS secondary endpoint. Does the read-access option make the upload succeed?
blocks.answer: No. The secondary is read-only for application access before a supported failover promotes it.
blocks.explanation: RA means read access, not an active writable second region. DNS, authorization, and application behavior must still be correct, and asynchronous lag still affects what a secondary read returns.

sections.title: Separate recovery objectives from replication mechanisms

blocks.text: A recovery point objective, RPO, is the amount of recent data the business can tolerate losing, expressed as time. Observed replication lag helps judge whether the design is meeting that objective. A recovery time objective, RTO, concerns how long the service may remain unavailable. Neither the seven-minute example nor RA access establishes a fixed RTO. Ordinary asynchronous redundancy must not be described as zero RPO. Separately enabled priority-replication offerings have specific eligibility and SLA conditions; this lesson assumes none of those optional guarantees.

Planned customer-managed failover requires both regions' storage endpoints to be available and coordinates replication to avoid expected data loss. Unplanned failover addresses an unavailable primary, accepts possible loss, and removes geo-redundancy until it is reconfigured. Failover operates at account scope and changes where the storage service endpoints lead; it does not fail over the website's virtual machines or database. It is not a general account-migration method. Check feature restrictions before either type rather than practicing on a production account.

Replication carries legitimate writes, mistaken overwrites, and applicable deletions. A geography change cannot recover a good document version that the protection design never retained. Versioning, soft delete, immutability where appropriate, and separately tested backups solve different recovery problems. A second copy is useful only if its content, access controls, retention, and restore procedure meet the requirement. The school must ask both 'can readers reach surviving data?' and 'can we restore yesterday's correct document?'

sections.title: Object replication is a selected relationship between accounts

blocks.text: Native object replication asynchronously copies eligible block blobs between a source account and a destination account. Unlike account geo-redundancy, you choose the participating accounts and containers, which can be in the same or different regions. It can distribute approved newsletters near another school's readers without copying every dataset in the original account. It is not automatic for every object when an account is created, and it does not replicate Azure Files shares, queues, tables, append blobs, page blobs, or blob snapshots.

items: Both accounts must be supported general-purpose v2 or premium block blob accounts. Both must have blob versioning enabled, and the source must also have change feed enabled. Versioning retains blob states; change feed records changes for the replication process.

Use flat namespaces. Current object replication does not support HNS-enabled accounts or blobs uploaded through Data Lake Storage APIs. The feature matrix also excludes HNS-related NFS and SFTP configurations.

Use eligible online blobs. Standard hot, cool, or cold blobs can participate, but moving either participating blob into Archive causes replication to fail. Rehydrating alone does not trigger replication; a subsequent data update is needed.

Microsoft-managed and customer-managed encryption keys are supported, but source blobs written with a customer-provided key are not. A customer-provided key sent on a request is different from a customer-managed Key Vault key.

Check the participating accounts' own redundancy restrictions. Premium block blob object replication does not give that account GRS. Archive incompatibility with ZRS and geo-zone configurations also remains a separate restriction.

blocks.text: The dedicated object replication overview states that customer-managed failover is unsupported for either participating account. A broader recovery page currently contains a conflicting unplanned-failover table entry. For this design, follow the explicit feature-specific restriction and do not promise that object replication and customer-managed failover can be combined. Confirm any changed support before designing around that combination. This is exactly why a feature's prerequisites deserve more attention than a product-name match.

sections.title: Policies identify accounts; rules identify the selected blobs

blocks.text: An object replication policy identifies the source and destination accounts. Each rule identifies a source container, a destination container, and optional selection filters. Both containers must exist. The policy must be associated with both accounts using the same policy ID and matching rule IDs. When configuring both sides through the portal's source-account workflow, the portal creates the corresponding destination policy. In a manual policy-file workflow, create the destination policy first and use its returned IDs on the source.

By default, a new rule copies only newly created blobs. To include the school's existing newsletters, deliberately select the all-objects copy scope or an appropriate creation-time scope. Prefix filters match the beginning of blob names, not an arbitrary filename search or wildcard expression. A prefix approved/ selects approved/newsletter.pdf but not drafts/approved-newsletter.pdf. Account redundancy has no such selective container rule: it operates according to the account's redundancy configuration.

Configuring the policy is a management operation requiring the documented Contributor-level permissions at the relevant account scope or higher, with permissions to configure the prerequisite blob service properties. Treat those permissions carefully because enabling replication causes data movement. If separate administrators own the accounts, they can exchange the policy definition rather than account keys. Use full Azure resource IDs to identify the accounts. New accounts created since December 15, 2023 disallow cross-tenant replication by default; inspect the actual setting instead of trusting older tutorial defaults. Our example stays within one Microsoft Entra tenant.

sections.title: Check the replication path, not just your laptop's connection

blocks.text: An administrator being able to open both accounts in the portal does not prove that data can move between them. Management access, data authorization, and network reachability are different checks. A private endpoint places a service-specific private address in a virtual network for clients using that path. It does not grant blob permissions, automatically disable the public endpoint, or establish a generic tunnel between two storage accounts. A public endpoint being enabled is also not the same as allowing anonymous blob reads.

For a source account with public network access disabled, do not assume that merely adding private endpoints proves native object replication will work. Microsoft's private-endpoint documentation explicitly describes supported REST-based copy tools such as AzCopy and Storage Explorer, including their need for access to both accounts. That is not an explicit guarantee for the background object replication service. The current object replication overview and configuration pages do not establish a universal source-public-endpoint requirement or a private-endpoint-only recipe. Treat that exact network combination as a support and verification gate, not as a reason to open a confidential source to all networks.

There is one clear current network incompatibility: native object replication is not supported when either participating account is associated with a network security perimeter. A perimeter is an additional isolation boundary for supported Azure services, not another name for a private endpoint. The documented configuration restrictions prevent combining it with object replication. For the paper example below, assume an approved compatible network configuration, no perimeter, and verified access to the required account endpoints. In a real restricted environment, confirm the exact service path, then verify replication status and the destination data before accepting the design.

sections.title: Worked example: distribute approved school newsletters

blocks.title: Copy the right objects without turning the destination into an editing area
blocks.scenario: Two fictional standard general-purpose v2 LRS accounts in the same tenant use flat namespaces, compatible networking without a security perimeter, and hot block blobs. The source container is documents; the destination container is published-copy. The school wants both existing and future approved newsletters, not drafts. This is a configuration walkthrough, not a live deployment.

steps.action: Verify blob type, account kind, namespace, online tier, network compatibility, and authorization before defining a rule.
steps.why: A perfect-looking policy cannot fix an unsupported blob type, HNS, an archived blob, a blocked path, or lack of authority over a participating account.

steps.action: Enable versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source; create the two containers if an authorized deployment is later approved.
steps.why: Replication uses source change information and versioned blob states. A destination change feed is not one of these required prerequisites.

steps.action: In the source account, open Data management, Object replication, then Create replication rules. Select the destination subscription and account, pair documents with published-copy, enter prefix approved/, and use the copy-scope Change control to select all objects.
steps.why: The prefix excludes drafts, while all-objects scope includes older eligible approved documents that the new-objects default would omit.

steps.action: After an approved configuration review, Save and apply would start the portal workflow and create the destination policy automatically. Alternatively, use the destination-first policy exchange and associate its returned IDs with the source.
steps.why: Two unrelated policy IDs do not form one replication relationship. Full resource IDs identify the intended accounts and support same-tenant checks. Saving starts billable data movement; this paper exercise stops before applying anything.

steps.action: Evaluate approved/june.pdf, approved/september.pdf, and drafts/september.pdf, assuming the first existed before the rule and the other two were added afterward.
steps.why: Both approved names are selected because all-objects scope includes the older one. The drafts name fails the prefix filter, regardless of its creation time.

steps.action: Inspect source-blob replication status and read the resulting destination objects; route later edits to the source.
steps.why: Asynchronous work is not complete merely because the policy exists. Direct application writes to a destination container under the active rule are blocked with a conflict response.

blocks.result: Two of the three candidate names are eligible: 1 older approved blob + 1 newer approved blob = 2. The draft is not eligible. Completion still depends on replication succeeding, and this distribution relationship does not automatically supply a backup policy or a failover plan.

sections.title: Understand the destination's state and its limits

blocks.text: Do not tell teachers that the destination is an ordinary writable mirror. While the container is governed by an active replication rule, direct writes fail. Reads and deletes are permitted subject to authorization and other protections. To write normally to that destination container, first remove the applicable rule or policy through an approved change. This is a data-governance decision, not a workaround to apply whenever an upload is inconvenient.

Source deletion also needs a precise explanation. With versioning enabled, deleting the current source blob leaves previous versions and no current version; object replication propagates that state. This does not mean every destructive action anywhere is safely reversible. It is not a promise to retain arbitrarily deleted containers, accounts, snapshots, or versions, nor does it restore a destination blob someone independently deletes. Destination versions receive their own version IDs. Plan retention and recovery separately, and test the exact deletion scenario the school must survive.

A change of the source access tier does not automatically set the same destination tier. Archive at either end can prevent later updates, and destination immutability can block replication operations even when the source change succeeds. Current blob index tag replication is a separately configured preview, so do not assume ordinary replication includes those tags. Check source status and destination content, not only a successful policy save. Costs include stored versions, operations, change-feed processing, and possible regional egress.

blocks.title: Three different reasons to have another copy
blocks.text: Account redundancy protects against infrastructure failures under the selected local and regional model. Object replication distributes selected supported block blobs under policies and rules. Backup and data-protection features preserve recoverable states according to retention and restore rules. The word 'copy' alone does not establish which of these requirements has been met.

checkpoints.prompt: A standard general-purpose v2 account in a supporting region must remain resilient to a zone outage, keep a regional replica, and allow Blob reads from that replica before failover. Archive tier is not required. Which option matches?

choices.text: RA-GZRS.
choices.explanation: Correct. It combines primary zone redundancy, an asynchronous regional replica, and secondary read access.

choices.text: GRS.
choices.explanation: GRS does not supply primary ZRS or direct secondary reads before failover.

choices.text: ZRS.
choices.explanation: ZRS supplies zonal protection in the primary region but no regional replica or secondary read endpoint.

choices.text: Premium block blob storage, regardless of redundancy.
choices.explanation: Performance does not imply the requested resilience. Premium block blob accounts do not provide the geo-redundant family.

checkpoints.explanation: Match all three requirements and the stated account, region, and tier qualifications.

checkpoints.prompt: At an outage at 10:12, Last Sync Time is 10:05. Writes completed at 10:03, 10:07, and 10:11. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: The 10:03 write is covered; later writes are uncertain, with a seven-minute exposure window.
choices.explanation: Correct. The boundary covers writes before 10:05, and 10:12 minus 10:05 equals seven minutes. Later writes may or may not have arrived.

choices.text: All writes are safe because local replication was synchronous.
choices.explanation: Synchronous primary replication does not make the transfer to the paired region synchronous.

choices.text: Exactly two documents are certainly lost, and failover takes seven minutes.
choices.explanation: Last Sync Time does not prove every later write is missing. The exposure interval is also not the failover duration.

checkpoints.explanation: Use Last Sync Time to reason about potential loss without inventing a loss count or recovery-time guarantee.

checkpoints.prompt: For ordinary native object replication between supported flat-namespace accounts, which TWO preparation statements are correct?

choices.text: Enable blob versioning on both source and destination.
choices.explanation: Correct. Both sides require versioning for the replication relationship.

choices.text: Enable change feed on the source and use eligible block blobs.
choices.explanation: Correct. Source change feed supplies change information; append and page blobs are not supported.

choices.text: Creating private endpoints alone proves the background replication path works, even with source public access disabled.
choices.explanation: A client private endpoint is not proof of the background service path. Validate the exact supported network configuration; do not confuse REST copy-tool support with an object replication guarantee.

choices.text: Enable HNS on the source to obtain the required versioning.
choices.explanation: Current HNS-enabled accounts do not support the required blob versioning and native object replication combination.

checkpoints.explanation: These are actual prerequisites. Network compatibility, account support, online tiers, and policy permissions remain additional gates.

checkpoints.prompt: An active rule uses prefix approved/ with all-objects scope. Which statement matches the worked newsletter example?

choices.text: The older and newer approved blobs are eligible; the draft is excluded, and direct writes to the destination container are blocked.
choices.explanation: Correct. The prefix and creation scope select the two approved names, while an active destination rule prevents ordinary application writes there.

choices.text: Only the newer approved blob is eligible because existing blobs can never be replicated.
choices.explanation: New-objects scope is the default, not a permanent limitation. This rule explicitly selects all-objects scope.

choices.text: All three blobs replicate and teachers can edit either copy independently.
choices.explanation: The draft fails the prefix filter, and the destination is not an independent editing area under an active replication rule.

checkpoints.explanation: Selection rules and destination write restrictions are both necessary to predict the result; replication is neither automatic for all objects nor a bidirectional collaboration feature.

takeaways: Local and zonal writes are synchronous; regional replication is asynchronous.
RA variants add secondary reads, not secondary writes or zero data loss.
Check service, account type, region, namespace, and tier before promising a redundancy option.
Object replication needs eligible block blobs, versioning at both ends, source change feed, and matching policies.
Select existing data and prefixes deliberately, and verify completion rather than assuming policy creation copied everything.
Replication is not backup, and a private endpoint is not proof that every background data movement feature is supported.

lessons.title: Protect stored data and transfer only what you intend
lessons.summary: Separate encryption at rest from secure transport, configure key ownership safely, and use Storage Explorer and AzCopy without confusing sign-in with permission or synchronization with backup.
objectives: Explain default server-side encryption and when customer-managed keys are appropriate.
Plan managed identity, Key Vault permissions, rotation, encryption scopes, and infrastructure encryption.
Separate Storage Explorer discovery and sign-in from actual blob data authorization.
Choose safe AzCopy transfer operations, preview changes, and verify both endpoints.

sections.title: A locked cupboard and a protected delivery route are different

blocks.text: Encryption changes readable data into a form that needs the right cryptographic key to recover its meaning. Azure Storage applies service-side encryption, often abbreviated SSE, automatically when it persists data. New accounts use Microsoft-managed keys by default. Encryption at rest is enabled for all storage accounts and cannot be disabled. It covers standard and premium performance, supported redundancy copies, and stored objects and metadata. You do not need to purchase Premium or select a customer-managed key just to make an ordinary blob encrypted at rest.

Azure decrypts data transparently for authorized reads. Consequently, encrypted storage does not make a carelessly public newsletter container private, and it does not stop an authorized user from deleting a document. Network rules determine whether the request can reach the service, data authorization determines whether it may perform the operation, and encryption protects stored bytes. A school application still needs to decide which signed-in teacher may see which document. None of those responsibilities disappears because storage encryption is automatic.

Transport Layer Security, TLS, protects the connection while data travels. HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS. For the Blob REST operations in this module, require secure transfer so ordinary HTTP requests are rejected, and configure the appropriate minimum TLS version, at least TLS 1.2 for this design. That is separate from encryption at rest. Infrastructure encryption, described below, adds another at-rest layer; it does not upgrade a network connection to HTTPS. Azure Files protocol-specific transport settings need their own review rather than assuming every protocol behaves like Blob REST.

sections.title: Customer-managed keys add control and responsibility

blocks.text: A customer-managed key, CMK, gives the school control over the key protecting the account's root data-encryption key. Azure still performs service-side encryption and decryption. The key is stored in Azure Key Vault or Key Vault Managed HSM, a managed hardware security module service, rather than pasted into the document uploader. Choose CMK for a genuine key-control, audit, or compliance requirement. Default Microsoft-managed keys remain an appropriate option when that additional responsibility is unnecessary.

For the same-tenant Key Vault design here, the vault must have soft delete and purge protection enabled. Soft delete keeps a deleted key recoverable for its retention period; purge protection prevents bypassing that period by permanently destroying it early. Supported keys are RSA or RSA-HSM with supported sizes of 2048, 3072, or 4096 bits. Those are cryptographic key sizes, not document-size limits. The storage service's identity needs get, wrapKey, and unwrapKey permissions on the key, with a network path that allows the key access.

A managed identity is an Azure-managed identity for a resource, avoiding a password embedded in a script. When configuring CMK while creating a storage account, use a user-assigned managed identity that already exists. For an existing account, either a user-assigned identity or its system-assigned identity can be used. The administrator's ability to select a vault is not the same as the storage identity's ability to use its key. Grant the latter permissions explicitly and verify them.

Account-level CMK configuration protects Blob Storage and Azure Files. Queue and Table data are not automatically switched to CMK merely because blobs use it; support for using the account encryption key for those services must be selected when the account is created. Cross-tenant key configurations have additional identity setup and are outside this worked same-tenant design. A customer-provided key, supplied with individual Blob requests, is another model and is not interchangeable with the Key Vault-backed CMK used here.

sections.title: Keep the key available while changing its version

blocks.text: Rotation creates a new key version according to the organization's policy. Azure Storage does not create that version for you; configure the rotation policy or perform the approved key-management operation in the key store. A version-pinned storage configuration continues using its specified version until you update it. A versionless configuration lets Storage check the vault daily and adopt a newer version. Do not treat creating a new key version as proof that every dependent account has already switched.

Microsoft instructs customers using automatic version updates to wait 24 hours before disabling the older version. Also verify adoption and working data access under the approved rotation procedure. Normal supported rotation changes protection of the account encryption key without requiring you to download and re-upload every PDF, and does not require downtime. However, disabling a needed key, removing identity permissions, or blocking vault access can make affected reads and writes fail. Key availability is part of the storage availability design, not merely a compliance checkbox.

blocks.prompt: An administrator creates a new Key Vault key version and immediately disables the older one. The storage account uses automatic version updates. Does automatic mean the account has already switched?
blocks.answer: No. Automatic updating is checked daily, not guaranteed at the instant the key version is created.
blocks.explanation: Follow the documented 24-hour waiting guidance and verify adoption before retiring the older version. Disabling the version still needed by Storage can interrupt data access even though the storage account, network, and user roles are otherwise correct.

sections.title: Choose the key boundary and any second encryption layer

blocks.text: By default, the encryption key boundary is the account. An encryption scope provides a separately configured key boundary for blobs within the account. A scope can use Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys. When creating a container, you can set a default scope for new blobs and either allow uploads to override it or require the container default. This can separate the key policies for general newsletters and more sensitive office documents without requiring every blob in the account to use one scope.

A scope is not a substitute for a role assignment or container privacy. A permitted reader still receives decrypted content while the scope and key are available. A disabled scope causes affected read and write operations to fail. Set the scope when uploading the blob; do not assume that adding a container default retroactively rewrites all existing objects. Blobs using encryption scopes cannot be placed in Archive under the documented restrictions. Scopes also have charges, including a minimum billing period, so they are not enabled in the optional learner lab.

Infrastructure encryption adds a second at-rest encryption layer using a separate Microsoft-managed key and algorithm. Service-level encryption can still use Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys. For whole-account infrastructure encryption, select it at account creation; it cannot be enabled or disabled afterward. The supported account types include general-purpose v2 and the specialized premium block blob, page blob, and file share accounts. This is not a setting for one TLS session.

There is an important scope-level distinction: if the account does not have infrastructure encryption, a new encryption scope can be created with infrastructure encryption for data using that scope. Its setting also cannot later be changed. If the whole account has infrastructure encryption, new scopes inherit it. Creating a new scope in an existing account therefore does not mean you have retroactively switched on infrastructure encryption for every existing blob. Match the actual boundary to the stated requirement.

sections.title: Worked example: meet a precise key-control requirement

blocks.title: Plan encryption for a new office document account
blocks.scenario: School policy requires a new standard general-purpose v2 Blob account to use a school-controlled key, whole-account double encryption at rest, and HTTPS transfers. The vault and account will be in the same tenant. No real key or resource is created in this exercise.

steps.action: Separate the three requirements into CMK, account-level infrastructure encryption, and secure transfer.
steps.why: Key control, a second at-rest layer, and transport encryption are different properties. Selecting only one cannot satisfy the other two.

steps.action: Prepare a supported RSA key in a vault with soft delete and purge protection, plus a user-assigned managed identity.
steps.why: Those vault protections and key types are prerequisites. New-account CMK configuration needs an identity available before the account exists.

steps.action: Grant that identity the necessary key operations and ensure the approved vault network path is usable.
steps.why: The storage service must obtain and use the wrapping key. An administrator being able to open the vault does not grant the service this ability.

steps.action: Select CMK and the prepared identity during creation, enable infrastructure encryption then, and require secure Blob REST transfers.
steps.why: Whole-account infrastructure encryption is a creation-time choice. The separate HTTPS requirement protects the transfer rather than the stored ciphertext.

steps.action: Choose and document automatic or pinned key-version updates, including the old-version retention and verification procedure.
steps.why: Rotation is an operational dependency. A pinned version needs explicit updating; automatic updating is daily rather than immediate.

steps.action: After any future approved deployment, inspect encryption properties and test a synthetic authorized upload and download without exposing the key.
steps.why: The settings verify intent, while the data test helps verify that the service identity, key availability, networking, and authorization work together.

blocks.result: The proposed design satisfies each requirement with its corresponding control. If this were an existing account without whole-account infrastructure encryption, the plan would need a new appropriately configured account and migration, not a nonexistent retroactive account toggle.

sections.title: Storage Explorer: being signed in is only the beginning

blocks.text: Azure Storage Explorer is a desktop application for browsing and operating on storage data. Use a current version and Microsoft Entra sign-in where supported. For our Blob examples, the identity needs Storage Blob Data Reader to list and download, or Storage Blob Data Contributor to upload and manage the intended blobs. These are data roles. Reader at the Azure resource level helps discover accounts but does not itself grant Blob data access.

The normal subscription tree needs management read access to discover accounts and their endpoints. A user with only a container-scoped data role can instead attach that container by its known URL through the Connect dialog and Microsoft Entra ID. This avoids granting broader account-management permissions just to make browsing convenient. The identity and tenant selected in the dialog must match the authorized principal. Allow for role-assignment propagation before diagnosing an immediately repeated failure.

Storage Explorer may use account keys if the signed-in user's management permissions allow retrieving them. For an identity-only Blob exercise, open Settings, Services, Storage Accounts, and enable Disable Usage of Keys, then verify the actual access method. This setting does not convert features that still require keys into identity-based features. Do not paste an account key or a signed access URL into lesson notes, screenshots, logs, or a support message. Keys can confer broad account data access; a successful key-based test would not prove that the intended data role works. These Blob role instructions are not a blanket claim that every Azure Files operation uses the same authorization model.

sections.title: AzCopy moves data in a chosen direction

blocks.text: AzCopy is a command-line transfer utility. Its login operation obtains a Microsoft Entra token; it does not assign any role. For an ordinary Blob-to-Blob transfer using that identity, arrange source read permission and destination write permission at the required scopes. Storage Blob Data Reader on the source and Storage Blob Data Contributor on the destination are suitable built-in choices for this example. The destination role includes more than upload alone, so keep its scope narrow. Local uploads instead need local-file read access and Azure destination permission.

A copy operation uploads, downloads, or copies selected data. It can overwrite destination objects depending on its options, so 'copy' does not mean harmless. It does not delete unrelated destination objects merely because they are absent from the source. A sync operation compares a chosen source with a destination and updates in one direction. By default, synchronization compares names and last-modified times; timestamps and the local computer's clock matter. It is not automatically a two-way collaboration system.

The dangerous difference appears when destination deletion is enabled for sync. Objects that exist only at the destination can then be removed. With deletion set to true there is no per-object confirmation; prompt requests confirmation, and false disables that destination-deletion behavior. Even false does not prevent overwriting a changed matching name. Preview with dry-run, check paths and direction, and use dedicated synthetic data before considering a real operation. A preview lists planned copies or removals without making those data changes, but may still read and enumerate remote resources and incur request charges.

blocks.explanation: Optional manual AzCopy v10 example, not Azure CLI and not executed by this course. Microsoft code-sample search grounded the login and sync patterns; the current AzCopy sync reference documents dry-run and deletion flags. Replace both placeholders with authorized sandbox values, create the local school-upload directory with synthetic files, and use the instructor-provided isolated container. Keep --dry-run. Login stores a token through the operating system's secret store; it supplies no data role. The second command only previews local-to-Blob synchronization and does not prove that a later write will be authorized.

sections.title: Worked example: copy an approved document without losing another

blocks.title: Use Storage Explorer and AzCopy to inspect the same transfer plan
blocks.scenario: The local school-upload directory contains announcement.txt. The approved sandbox destination container contains keep.txt, which is not in that local directory. Neither contains student records. The task is to add announcement.txt while keeping keep.txt. Network access is available, and the learner has a container-scoped Blob data role.

steps.action: Sign into the correct tenant in Storage Explorer and attach the known container URL if account discovery is unavailable.
steps.why: A narrow data role can permit container access without permission to list every account in the subscription. Missing discovery is not automatically missing data authorization.

steps.action: Inspect the two locations and state the intended direction: local directory to Blob container.
steps.why: A reversed direction changes the destination and can change which files are overwritten or deleted. The destination-only keep.txt is deliberate, not clutter.

steps.action: Use the AzCopy login and dry-run pattern above with destination deletion explicitly false.
steps.why: The preview exposes the planned scope without changing blobs. It should plan the missing announcement.txt and must not plan deletion of keep.txt.

steps.action: Prefer an explicit single-file copy or a Storage Explorer upload with an appropriate overwrite choice for the eventual authorized transfer.
steps.why: The requirement is to add a document, not to make the whole destination identical to a local folder. There is no reason to enable destructive synchronization.

steps.action: After an optional approved upload, inspect the operation result, refresh the destination, and download the synthetic object for comparison.
steps.why: A completed sign-in or dry run is not proof of a successful data write. The transferred content must match, and keep.txt must still exist.

steps.action: For a future account-to-account copy, additionally verify source read permission, destination write permission, and both network paths.
steps.why: AzCopy can arrange server-to-server transfers. Its client and the transfer method still need the documented account reachability. A working source read does not establish destination access, especially with private endpoints and firewalls.

blocks.result: With successful upload, the destination contains announcement.txt and keep.txt: its original 1 object plus 1 new object equals 2. A dry run alone leaves only the original object. Enabling destination deletion for synchronization would threaten keep.txt because it is absent from the source, contrary to the requirement.

sections.title: Diagnose the layer that failed before changing permissions

blocks.text: If the container cannot be listed, first record the exact account, container, selected identity, tenant, operation, and error. Check endpoint resolution and network reachability separately from token validity and data roles. A successful browser login proves authentication happened, not that the firewall permits the data connection. A forbidden response can reflect several authorization or policy conditions, so do not fix every failure by granting subscription Owner, enabling anonymous access, or pasting an account key.

If reads work but writes fail, check the destination's role scope, an active object replication rule, leases or immutability restrictions where applicable, and encryption key or scope availability. A replication destination rejects direct writes even for an otherwise authorized operator. For an HNS-enabled account, directory ACLs can also affect access; the examples here deliberately use flat namespaces. Use the operation's result and logs to choose the next check, and never publish logs containing secrets.

blocks.title: Identify the control that actually satisfies the requirement
blocks.text: Microsoft-managed keys already provide encryption at rest. CMK adds customer key control, encryption scopes narrow key boundaries, infrastructure encryption adds a second at-rest layer, and HTTPS protects transport. Storage Explorer and AzCopy sign-in authenticate an identity; data roles authorize operations. Copy and sync move data, but only deliberately configured recovery protection supplies a dependable restore path.

checkpoints.prompt: Policy requires a new standard Blob account to have both whole-account double encryption at rest and encrypted REST transfers. Which plan satisfies both?

choices.text: Enable infrastructure encryption at account creation and require HTTPS transfers.
choices.explanation: Correct. Infrastructure encryption supplies the second at-rest layer, while secure transfer protects Blob REST traffic.

choices.text: Require HTTPS, which also adds the second infrastructure encryption layer.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects transit. It does not configure infrastructure encryption for stored data.

choices.text: Create the account with ordinary settings and enable whole-account infrastructure encryption next month.
choices.explanation: Whole-account infrastructure encryption must be selected at creation and cannot be toggled afterward.

checkpoints.explanation: Different protection boundaries require separate controls; default service-side encryption remains present in every case.

checkpoints.prompt: For same-tenant CMK configuration during new-account creation, which TWO preparations are valid?

choices.text: Use a supported RSA key in a vault with soft delete and purge protection.
choices.explanation: Correct. Key type and vault recovery protections are documented prerequisites.

choices.text: Prepare a user-assigned managed identity with the necessary key permissions and network access.
choices.explanation: Correct. New-account CMK configuration needs that existing identity, and the service must be able to get, wrap, and unwrap the key.

choices.text: Plan to disable an older key version immediately after creating its replacement because automatic updates are instantaneous.
choices.explanation: Automatic storage updates are checked daily. Follow the 24-hour waiting guidance and verify adoption before disabling the older version.

choices.text: Paste the account access key into every PDF upload script to configure encryption.
choices.explanation: An account access key is an authorization secret, not the Key Vault CMK configuration. Embedding it spreads broad credentials and does not satisfy these prerequisites.

checkpoints.explanation: CMK depends on a supported protected key store and an authorized service identity, with a safe continuing rotation process.

checkpoints.prompt: A user can sign in and discover storage accounts but cannot download a private blob. Assume the correct endpoint and network path work and no special policy blocks the read. Which missing permission is the relevant next check?

choices.text: A Blob data-read role at the source container or a containing scope.
choices.explanation: Correct. Storage Blob Data Reader is an appropriate built-in role for the stated download operation.

choices.text: Only Reader on the subscription, because all management readers can download blobs.
choices.explanation: Reader permits management discovery but does not itself authorize Blob data reads.

choices.text: Premium performance, because standard storage cannot be used with Storage Explorer.
choices.explanation: Storage Explorer supports the standard Blob scenario. Performance tier is not the missing data authorization.

checkpoints.explanation: Authentication, account discovery, network access, and data authorization must be evaluated separately.

checkpoints.prompt: The destination has keep.txt; the local source has only announcement.txt. The requirement is to add the announcement and preserve keep.txt. What is the safest plan described in this lesson?

choices.text: Preview the exact scope without deletion, then use an approved explicit upload or copy and verify both objects.
choices.explanation: Correct. It checks direction and intended changes without treating the destination-only object as disposable.

choices.text: Enable destination deletion during sync to ensure keep.txt is protected.
choices.explanation: The opposite is true: destination-only keep.txt becomes a deletion candidate when destination deletion is enabled.

choices.text: Stop after dry-run and report that announcement.txt was uploaded.
choices.explanation: Dry-run does not copy the file. It is a preview, not proof of completed transfer or write authorization.

checkpoints.explanation: A safe transfer plan protects intentional destination-only data and distinguishes a preview from an executed, verified operation.

takeaways: Storage encrypts at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys; transport protection is separate.
Customer-managed keys require protected key storage, the right managed identity, permissions, reachability, and careful rotation.
Encryption scopes and infrastructure encryption have different boundaries and creation-time restrictions.
Successful sign-in and account discovery do not establish Blob data authorization.
For account-to-account transfers, verify source reads, destination writes, and both network paths.
Preview synchronization, avoid unintended destination deletion and overwrites, and verify actual transfer results without exposing secrets.

glossary.definition: An Azure resource that provides a namespace and shared configuration for its supported storage services.
A Blob Storage object type suited to documents and other ordinary objects; the type supported by native object replication.
An account's product family, such as StorageV2, BlockBlobStorage, or FileStorage, interpreted together with performance and supported features.
A product configuration identifier. For storage, a value such as Standard_ZRS combines performance and redundancy.
A namespace with real directory semantics for Data Lake Storage, with feature compatibility different from flat blob names.
An independently powered, cooled, and networked location within an Azure region that supports zones.
Replication that completes the required local or zonal copies before acknowledging a successful write.
Replication that can lag behind an acknowledged source write, allowing a destination to contain an older state.
Recovery point objective: the business's tolerated interval of recent data loss, not the time needed to restart service.
The geo-replication boundary before which writes are confirmed available in the secondary; later writes can be uncertain.
A relationship between source and destination accounts containing rules for eligible block blobs and container pairs.
A record of blob changes used by features such as native object replication; required on its source account.
A customer-controlled key in Key Vault or Managed HSM protecting the storage account's encryption key, with ongoing access and rotation responsibilities.
An Azure-managed identity a resource can use to authenticate without an embedded application password.
A Blob Storage key-management boundary applied to individual blobs or used as a container's default for new uploads.
A separate second at-rest encryption layer using Microsoft-managed keys, selected when creating the account or applicable scope.
Permission to perform a data operation such as reading or writing a blob, distinct from discovering or configuring the account.
A preview of an operation's planned changes. AzCopy sync dry-run does not perform the planned copies or removals, though it can enumerate remote data.
